title: Does Islam Permit a Man to Hit His Wife? Quran 4:34 Explained | Real Talk | Dr. Tesneem Alkiek
description:

Islam condemns domestic violence, and a woman is never required to stay silent in the face of abuse. So how do we make sense of Quran 4:34, the verse Muslim women often wrestle with?

Yaqeen scholar Dr. Tesneem Alkiek and host Cadar Mohamud start with a key principle in the Islamic legal tradition: marriage never erased a woman’s independent legal identity. She owns property, enters contracts, and can take her husband to court when she is harmed. Dr. Alkiek explains how jurists defined that harm.

She then looks at what classical jurists actually said about physical discipline. That includes the strict limits they placed on it and how many of them advised men to avoid it entirely. The episode ends with the Prophet’s ﷺ example and what a woman should do when patience is the wrong response.

description:
He marched in the Prophet’s ﷺ army, waiting for his chance to kill him.

Shayba ibn Uthman (ra) lost his father, his uncle and his cousins in a single day at Uhud. It is narrated that at Hunayn, when the Muslim lines broke and people fled, he found himself right behind the Prophet ﷺ with nothing between them but his sword. What happened next turned the man who came for revenge into one reported to have stood his ground beside the Prophet ﷺ. He later became a keeper of the Ka’bah, and his family holds its keys to this day.

Grief can harden into a hatred with every reason behind it. The Prophet ﷺ answered this one with a hand on the chest instead of a sword, then told Shaybah that Allah had intended better for him than he had intended for himself.

title: Aging Parents, Growing Kids and "InshaAllah Next Year" | Khutbah by Dr. Omar Suleiman
description:
You may still be alive tomorrow, but this version of your life won’t be.

Your body will change. Your circumstances will change. Your children will grow older. Your parents may not always be here. The person waiting for your apology may eventually stop waiting.

So what happens to all the good we keep telling ourselves we’ll do later?

The call we keep meaning to make. The apology we keep putting off. The time we assume we’ll have with our parents and children. The charity we tell ourselves we’ll give tomorrow.
The Qur’an preserves the plea of someone who ran out of time:

“My Lord, if only You would delay me for a little while, I would give in charity and be among the righteous.” — (Surah Al-Munafiqun, Verse 10)

But the delay never comes.

This isn’t simply a warning about dying suddenly. It’s a reminder that some of the good we postpone depends on having the right person, the right moment, or the right opportunity still in front of us.

In this khutbah, Dr. Omar Suleiman reflects on time, aging parents, growing children, unfinished apologies, and the opportunities for goodness we assume will still be there tomorrow.
What have you been putting off because you assume you’ll have more time?

title: The Eclipse Prayer | Dr. Omar Suleiman
description:
There was an eclipse on one of the most painful days of the Prophet ﷺ's life. He reminded the ummah about the eclipse prayer.

How to pray Salat al-Kusuf (the eclipse prayer):

It's 2 rak’ahs, prayed in congregation if possible. No adhan or iqamah.

In each rak’ah: Recite Surah al-Fatihah + a long surah, then a long ruku, then rise and recite al-Fatihah + another surah again, then bow a second time, then go into sujood as normal. So each rak’ah has 2 standings, 2 bowings, and 2 prostrations.

After the prayer, it's sunnah to give a khutbah reminding people of Allah's power, as the Prophet ﷺ did. 

Beyond the prayer, it's sunnah to make du’a and dhikr until the eclipse ends, give charity, and seek Allah’s forgiveness.

title: Safwan ibn al-Mu’attal (ra): Slandered for Helping A Woman | The Firsts | Dr. Omar Suleiman
description:
Safwan ibn al-Muattal (ra) was a Bedouin warrior from Banu Sulaym, trusted with the most exposed job in the army: staying behind everyone else to make sure no one got left in the desert. When he found the wife of the Prophet ﷺ alone and asleep, left behind by accident, he said exactly one sentence the entire journey back to Medina.

That silence should have protected him. Instead, it became the center of one of the most damaging rumors in early Islamic history, and he was never even asked to defend himself before it spread.

What the Prophet ﷺ said about him, and what he let Safwan (ra) do to the man who started the rumor, is not what you'd expect.

Discover the story of the companion history almost left out of his own scandal, the cost of being slandered while doing exactly the right thing, and what the Prophet ﷺ's response teaches about restoring a man's honor without ever needing him to ask for it.

title: Before the Answer
description:
There’s a difference between wanting something from someone and wanting to be close to them. Most of us approach du’a like a request form. We ask for the job, the marriage, the relief, the outcome. And when the outcome is delayed, we think the relationship is distant.

But think about the people you love most. Sometimes the gift isn’t what they give you. It’s the fact that you’re with them.

Allah says you ask and He is close. Then He says you ask and He answers. Nearness comes before response. Love comes before provision.

So ask for what you need. Just don’t forget that the greatest thing He can give you isn’t what’s in your hands. It’s where you stand.
